questions.stem: Which of these is a pure substance?
options: Brass alloy
Distilled water
Sea water
Air
questions.explanation: Distilled water contains only water molecules, so it is a pure compound. Sea water and air are mixtures of several substances, and brass is an alloy, a mixture of copper and zinc.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a compound from a mixture?
options: A compound has a fixed composition; a mixture's composition can vary
A compound can be separated by filtration; a mixture cannot be separated
A compound contains one type of atom; a mixture contains several types
A compound melts over a range of temperatures; a mixture melts sharply
questions.explanation: A compound contains elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio, such as H₂O. A mixture's components are not chemically bonded and can be present in any proportion. One type of atom describes an element, not a compound.

questions.stem: Which of these is a heterogeneous mixture?
options: Vinegar from a bottle
Sand stirred into water
Sugar dissolved in water
Air in a sealed flask
questions.explanation: In a heterogeneous mixture the composition is not uniform and the separate parts can be seen, like sand grains in water. A solution such as sugar water, air or vinegar is homogeneous, with the same composition throughout.

questions.stem: A student measures the melting point of a sample of a solid that is known to melt at 122 °C when pure. The sample melts gradually between 115 °C and 119 °C. What is the best conclusion?
options: The sample is pure, because it melted within a few degrees of the known value
The sample is a different pure compound, because it melts below 122 °C
The thermometer reads too high, because the sample melted early in the test
The sample is impure, because impurities lower and broaden the melting range
questions.explanation: A pure substance melts sharply at a fixed temperature. Impurities usually lower the melting point and make it melt over a range, which matches this sample. A thermometer reading too high would make the sample appear to melt at a higher temperature, not a lower one.

questions.stem: Which method would best separate a mixture of iron filings and sulfur powder?
options: Attracting the iron with a magnet
Filtering the mixture through paper
Distilling the mixture in a flask
Heating the mixture strongly in air
questions.explanation: Iron is magnetic and sulfur is not, so a magnet separates them by a physical property. Heating them together would make them react to form iron(II) sulfide, a compound, rather than separate them.

questions.stem: Ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) is dissolved in water (boiling point 100 °C). Which method separates them, and which property does it rely on?
options: Using a separating funnel, relying on their different densities in layers
Evaporation, relying on their different solubilities in water
Fractional distillation, relying on their different boiling points
Filtration, relying on the different sizes of their molecules
questions.explanation: Ethanol and water are miscible, so a separating funnel will not work, and filter paper lets both pass. Fractional distillation separates them because ethanol, with the lower boiling point, vaporises first.

questions.stem: Which method is used to obtain solid copper(II) sulfate from its aqueous solution?
options: Evaporation and crystallisation
Filtration
Simple distillation of the solid
Magnetic separation
questions.explanation: The copper(II) sulfate is dissolved, so it passes through filter paper. Evaporating some of the water and letting the solution cool allows crystals to form. Distillation would recover the water rather than the solid.

questions.stem: Oil and water form two separate layers. What is the simplest way to separate them?
options: Run off the lower layer through a separating funnel
Pour the whole mixture through filter paper in a funnel
Evaporate the oil and keep the water left behind
Dissolve the oil in more water and then distil it
questions.explanation: Immiscible liquids of different densities form layers, and the denser lower layer can be drained off through the tap of a separating funnel. Filtration separates insoluble solids from liquids, not two liquids.

questions.stem: Which model describes the structure of solid sodium chloride?
options: Sodium and chlorine atoms sharing pairs of electrons in a network
A lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by strong electrostatic attraction
NaCl molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces
Na⁺ ions in a sea of delocalised electrons released by the chlorine
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride is ionic: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are arranged in a three-dimensional crystal lattice, held by strong attraction between oppositely charged ions in all directions. There are no separate NaCl molecules.

questions.stem: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity, while molten sodium chloride does?
options: In the solid the ions are too small; melting makes the ions large enough to move
In the solid the ions are fixed in place; when molten the ions are free to move
In the solid the electrons are fixed; when molten the delocalised electrons can move
In the solid there are no ions; melting breaks covalent bonds to form ions
questions.explanation: Conduction needs mobile charged particles. Solid NaCl contains ions, but they are held in fixed positions in the lattice. Melting or dissolving frees the ions to move. Ionic compounds do not have delocalised electrons.

questions.stem: Why are ionic crystals brittle, shattering when struck?
options: The ions are held by weak forces that break as soon as any force is applied
The delocalised electrons escape from the lattice when it is struck sharply
Each ion is bonded to only one other ion, so the lattice has no strength
A shift in the layers brings ions of the same charge together, and they repel
questions.explanation: A blow can push one layer of ions along by one position, so like charges line up next to each other. The strong repulsion splits the crystal. The ionic bonds themselves are strong, which is why ionic compounds have high melting points.

questions.stem: Magnesium oxide melts at about 2850 °C, but sodium chloride melts at 801 °C. Which explanation is best?
options: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry larger charges, so the attraction between them is stronger
Magnesium oxide has covalent bonds, which are always stronger than ionic bonds
Magnesium oxide has delocalised electrons that hold its lattice together
Sodium chloride is made of molecules held by weak intermolecular forces
questions.explanation: Both are ionic lattices. The electrostatic attraction is stronger between ions with larger charges, and Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ are also smaller than Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so more energy is needed to separate them. Neither compound is molecular.

questions.stem: Which model describes metallic bonding?
options: A lattice of cations and anions held by electrostatic attraction
Neutral atoms sharing fixed pairs of electrons with their neighbours
Separate molecules held together by weak dispersion forces
A lattice of cations surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: In a metal, atoms release their valence electrons, which become delocalised throughout a lattice of positive ions. The bond is the attraction between the cations and these mobile electrons. Cations with anions describes an ionic lattice.

questions.stem: Why can metals be hammered into sheets without shattering, while ionic solids shatter?
options: Metals have weaker bonds than ionic solids, so their layers bend instead of breaking
Metal atoms share electron pairs in fixed directions that rearrange when struck
Metals contain anions that cancel any repulsion between neighbouring cations
Metal cations can slide past each other while still held by delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: Metallic bonding is non-directional: when layers of cations slide, the delocalised electrons move with them and keep holding the lattice together. In an ionic solid, sliding brings like charges together and the crystal splits. Many metals have very strong bonding, so weakness is not the reason.

questions.stem: Which property is explained by the delocalised electrons in a metal?
options: Conductivity only when the solid is melted
Poor heat conduction compared with glass
Low melting points for all metallic elements
Good electrical conductivity in the solid state
questions.explanation: Delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice, so metals conduct electricity as solids, and they also carry heat well. Conducting only when molten is typical of ionic compounds. Many metals, such as iron, have high melting points.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes ionic bonding from metallic bonding?
options: Ionic bonding is between metal atoms only; metallic bonding is between metal and non-metal atoms
Ionic bonding involves delocalised electrons; metallic bonding involves electrons transferred to anions
Ionic bonding is directional and weak; metallic bonding is directional and always strong
Ionic bonding is attraction between cations and anions; metallic is between cations and mobile electrons
questions.explanation: In ionic bonding, electrons are transferred from metal to non-metal atoms, forming cations and anions that attract. In metallic bonding, valence electrons are delocalised and attract the remaining cations. Both bonds act in all directions.

questions.stem: In a covalent bond, what holds the two atoms together?
options: Attraction between a positive ion and a negative ion next to each other
Attraction between cations and a sea of delocalised electrons
Attraction between two neighbouring molecules with permanent dipoles
Attraction of both nuclei to a shared pair of electrons between them
questions.explanation: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons in the region between two nuclei, with both nuclei strongly attracted to it. Attraction between molecules is an intermolecular force, which is much weaker than a covalent bond.

questions.stem: Methane melts at −182 °C even though its C-H covalent bonds are strong. Why?
options: Melting only overcomes the weak forces between molecules, not the covalent bonds
Melting breaks the C-H bonds, but these are much weaker than ionic bonds
Methane is a covalent network, and networks have low melting points
Methane contains delocalised electrons that weaken its covalent bonds
questions.explanation: In a covalent molecular substance, the strong covalent bonds are inside each molecule. Melting and boiling only separate the molecules from each other, which needs little energy because the intermolecular forces are weak. The methane molecules stay intact.

questions.stem: Silicon dioxide melts at about 1700 °C, while carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature. Why is there such a difference?
options: SiO₂ is ionic, while CO₂ has covalent bonds between its atoms
SiO₂ molecules are much heavier, so their intermolecular forces are stronger
SiO₂ has metallic bonding, while CO₂ has covalent bonding
SiO₂ is a covalent network; melting it breaks strong covalent bonds
questions.explanation: Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent network in which every atom is covalently bonded to its neighbours, so melting requires breaking many strong covalent bonds. Carbon dioxide is made of small separate molecules held by weak dispersion forces. Silicon dioxide has no discrete molecules.

questions.stem: A substance has these properties: melting point above 3500 °C, extremely hard, does not conduct electricity as a solid or when heated. Which structure fits best?
options: A molecular solid such as iodine
A covalent network such as diamond
An ionic lattice such as calcium oxide
A metallic lattice such as tungsten
questions.explanation: A very high melting point with no conduction under any conditions points to a covalent network, with no mobile charges at all. An ionic compound would conduct when molten, a metal conducts as a solid, and a molecular solid has a low melting point.

questions.stem: A table gives data for four substances. Which substance is most likely ionic?
options: Z: melts at 1414 °C, conducts poorly as a solid, insoluble in water
W: melts at 770 °C, conducts when molten or dissolved, not as a solid
X: melts at 1085 °C, conducts as a solid and when molten
Y: melts at 114 °C, does not conduct as a solid or as a liquid
questions.explanation: Ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct only when their ions are free to move, when molten or dissolved, which matches W. X behaves like a metal (it is copper's data), Y like a molecular solid, and Z like a covalent network semiconductor such as silicon.

questions.stem: What are allotropes?
options: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons in the nucleus
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements
Different elements that have the same arrangement of atoms in a solid
Different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state
questions.explanation: Allotropes are different structural forms of one element, such as diamond, graphite and the fullerenes for carbon. Atoms differing in neutrons are isotopes, and compounds with the same formula but different structures are isomers.

questions.stem: Why is diamond extremely hard and a non-conductor of electricity?
options: Its carbon atoms have lost electrons to form a lattice of C⁴⁺ ions
Each carbon is covalently bonded to four others, leaving no free electrons
Each carbon is bonded to three others in layers held by weak forces
Its carbon atoms form separate small molecules held by strong dispersion forces
questions.explanation: In diamond every carbon atom forms four strong covalent bonds in a rigid three-dimensional network, so it is very hard, and all four valence electrons are in localised bonds, so none can carry a current. Three bonds per carbon in layers describes graphite.

questions.stem: Graphite conducts electricity and is soft enough to use as a lubricant. Which structural feature explains both properties?
options: Layers of carbons each bonded to three others, with delocalised electrons and weak forces between layers
A three-dimensional network in which every carbon atom forms four strong covalent bonds to its neighbours
Separate C₆₀ molecules shaped like hollow spheres that can roll past each other and carry electrons
A lattice of carbon cations surrounded by delocalised electrons that holds all of the layers rigidly in place
questions.explanation: In graphite each carbon bonds to three others in flat hexagonal layers, and the fourth electron is delocalised along the layer, so graphite conducts. The layers are held together only by weak forces, so they slide over each other easily.

questions.stem: Graphene is best described as:
options: a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in hexagons
a hollow sphere of 60 carbon atoms joined in rings
a three-dimensional network of tetrahedral carbons
a stack of carbon layers held together by weak forces
questions.explanation: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, one atom thick, with each carbon bonded to three others in a hexagonal sheet. It has delocalised electrons, so it conducts electricity, and it is very strong. A sphere of 60 carbons is a fullerene, and a stack of layers is graphite.

questions.stem: Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, has a far lower melting point than diamond or graphite. Why?
options: Its carbon atoms are bonded by weaker covalent bonds than those found in diamond
Each carbon in C₆₀ forms only two bonds, so its molecules break apart easily on heating
It is an ionic solid made of C₆₀ ions, and its ions are held only loosely in the lattice
It is made of discrete molecules, so only weak forces between molecules are overcome
questions.explanation: Diamond and graphite are giant covalent networks, so melting means breaking covalent bonds. C₆₀ is a covalent molecular substance: its molecules are held together by weaker dispersion forces, which need far less energy to overcome. Each carbon in C₆₀ bonds to three others.

questions.stem: Which list contains only giant covalent network substances?
options: Diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide
Diamond, iodine and silicon dioxide
Graphite, sodium chloride and silicon
Sulfur, diamond and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide all have atoms covalently bonded in continuous networks. Iodine, sulfur (S₈) and carbon dioxide are molecular, and sodium chloride is ionic.

questions.stem: What is meant by describing an alkane as saturated?
options: It contains a ring of carbon atoms with delocalised electrons
It contains only single carbon-carbon bonds
It contains at least one carbon-carbon double bond
It has dissolved in water until no more will dissolve
questions.explanation: A saturated hydrocarbon has only single C-C bonds, so each carbon holds the maximum number of hydrogen atoms. Alkenes, with a C=C double bond, are unsaturated.

questions.stem: Which molecular formula belongs to an alkene?
options: C₆H₆
C₅H₁₂
C₄H₈
C₄H₁₀
questions.explanation: Alkenes with one double bond have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ, so C₄H₈ (butene) fits. C₄H₁₀ and C₅H₁₂ fit CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and are alkanes, and C₆H₆ is benzene.

questions.stem: Orange-brown bromine water is shaken separately with hexane and with hex-1-ene at room temperature, in the dark. What is observed?
options: Hexane decolourises it quickly; hex-1-ene leaves it orange-brown
Both decolourise it quickly, because both are hydrocarbons
Neither decolourises it, because bromine water only reacts with benzene
Hex-1-ene decolourises it quickly; hexane leaves it orange-brown
questions.explanation: The C=C double bond in an alkene reacts readily with bromine in an addition reaction, so the colour disappears quickly. Alkanes have only single bonds and react with bromine only slowly by substitution, usually in ultraviolet light. This is the standard test to tell alkenes from alkanes.

questions.stem: Ethene reacts with bromine to form 1,2-dibromoethane, C₂H₄Br₂. What type of reaction is this?
options: Substitution
Combustion
Decomposition
Addition
questions.explanation: The double bond opens and a bromine atom adds to each carbon, so all the atoms end up in one product. This is an addition reaction, typical of unsaturated alkenes. In substitution, as with alkanes, a hydrogen atom is replaced and HBr is also formed.

questions.stem: Methane reacts with chlorine in ultraviolet light to form chloromethane and hydrogen chloride. What type of reaction is this?
options: Neutralisation
Polymerisation
Substitution
Addition
questions.explanation: A chlorine atom replaces a hydrogen atom, and the displaced hydrogen leaves as HCl. Saturated alkanes have no double bond to add across, so they react by substitution, and only slowly, needing UV light.

questions.stem: Benzene, C₆H₆, has a high ratio of carbon to hydrogen, like an unsaturated compound, yet it does not readily decolourise bromine water. Why?
options: It contains only single carbon-carbon bonds, so it is a saturated hydrocarbon like hexane
It has three separate double bonds that are too far apart to react with bromine molecules
Its molecules are ionic, so they cannot react with covalent molecules such as bromine
Its ring of delocalised electrons is stable, so it tends to undergo substitution, not addition
questions.explanation: Benzene's six carbons form a ring in which six electrons are delocalised around the whole ring rather than fixed in three double bonds. This arrangement is especially stable, so benzene resists addition and reacts by substitution instead. It is not saturated, which its formula shows.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly links bonding to chemical properties for these hydrocarbons?
options: Alkanes react readily by addition because their single bonds break easily
Benzene is more reactive than alkenes because it contains more double bonds
Alkanes and alkenes react identically because both contain only C and H
Alkenes react readily by addition at the C=C bond; alkanes are less reactive
questions.explanation: The C=C double bond in an alkene is a reactive site where atoms can add. Alkanes contain only strong, unreactive C-C and C-H single bonds. Benzene's delocalised ring is less reactive towards addition than an alkene's double bond.

questions.stem: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
options: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂
CₙHₙ
CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
CₙH₂ₙ
questions.explanation: Alkanes have only single bonds, so for n carbons there are 2n + 2 hydrogens, as in methane CH₄ and propane C₃H₈. CₙH₂ₙ is the formula for alkenes with one double bond.

questions.stem: Nanomaterials are made of particles in which size range?
options: 0.01 to 0.1 nanometres
1 to 100 nanometres
1 to 100 micrometres
100 to 1000 nanometres
questions.explanation: Nanoparticles are between 1 and 100 nm across. At this size a large share of their atoms are at the surface, so they can have properties different from the same material in bulk. A tenth of a nanometre is about the size of a single atom.

questions.stem: Why can a nanoparticle form of a material behave differently from the same material in bulk?
options: Its atoms are made of different isotopes from those in the bulk form of the material
Its bonding changes from covalent to ionic once particles become small enough
Its particles are too small to have any surface, so they cannot react with anything
Its very large surface area to volume ratio exposes far more atoms at the surface
questions.explanation: As particles get smaller, the surface area to volume ratio rises sharply, so a much larger share of atoms sit at the surface and can react or interact with light. This is why nanoparticles can be better catalysts or look a different colour. The atoms and bonding are the same.
